question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [British presidency / settlement — its location and founding]
options: Bombay Presidency — west coast of India; ceded to Britain by Portugal as part of the dowry of Catherine of Braganza in 1661
Madras Presidency — Coromandel Coast (Bay of Bengal); Fort St. George established in 1639
Bengal Presidency — eastern India; headquartered at Calcutta (Fort William), developed as a major British centre after the Battle of Plassey (1757)
Surat Presidency — Gujarat coast; the British first established a factory at Surat in 1600, making it their earliest Indian base
wrong_fact: The British established their first factory at Surat in 1608–1613, not in 1600. The East India Company received its charter in 1600, but the first English factory at Surat was established in 1613 after Captain Thomas Best's naval victory over the Portuguese at the Battle of Swally (Suvali) in 1612. Also, Surat was not a 'Presidency' — Bombay, Madras, and Bengal were the three Presidencies; Surat was an early factory that later became subordinate to Bombay.
explanation: The English East India Company was granted its royal charter by Queen Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600. The first factory at Surat was established in 1613. Surat served as the headquarters of English India until it was superseded by Bombay in 1687. Bombay was ceded by Portugal in 1661; Madras (Fort St. George) was founded in 1639; Calcutta (Fort William) became the key Bengal centre after 1690 and was rebuilt after Plassey.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [British military/political action — location and significance in the context of Anglo-French rivalry]
options: Robert Clive's capture of Arcot (1751) — Arcot (Carnatic region); turned the tide against Chanda Sahib and demonstrated British resolve against French-backed candidates
Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) — Palashi, Bengal; Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daula (backed by French officers) and established British supremacy in Bengal
Battle of Wandiwash (22 January 1760) — near Vellore, Tamil Nadu; Eyre Coote defeated Lally, capturing Bussy and ending organised French military resistance
Siege and capture of Pondicherry (1761) — British forces under Sir Eyre Coote besieged Pondicherry; the French garrison surrendered and the town was razed
wrong_fact: The Battle of Wandiwash was NOT fought near Vellore. It was fought near the town of Vandavasi (Wandiwash) in the North Arcot district, which is roughly 100 km south-west of Madras — not near Vellore. Also, while Bussy was indeed captured at Wandiwash, the statement is otherwise broadly correct about Coote's decisive victory.
explanation: Wandiwash (Vandavasi) is located in the present-day Tiruvannamalai district of Tamil Nadu, not near Vellore. The battle on 22 January 1760 saw Sir Eyre Coote defeat the Comte de Lally; Bussy was captured, and the French retreated to Pondicherry, which was besieged and surrendered in January 1761. The other options are correctly stated: Arcot (1751) showed British fighting ability, and Plassey (1757) gave Britain Bengal.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [British diplomatic/territorial gain — the region acquired and the mechanism]
options: Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa (1765) — granted to the British EIC by Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II after the Battle of Buxar; gave Britain the right to collect revenue from these provinces
Northern Circars — acquired by the British from the Nizam of Hyderabad under Warren Hastings (1765–1766), displacing earlier French influence established by Bussy
Madras (Fort St. George) — returned to Britain by France under the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) in exchange for French retention of Louisbourg in North America
Bombay — acquired by Britain from the Dutch East India Company (VOC) in 1661 as part of negotiations following the Anglo-Dutch Wars
wrong_fact: Bombay was NOT acquired from the Dutch East India Company. Bombay was part of the dowry of the Portuguese Princess Catherine of Braganza when she married King Charles II of England in 1661. Portugal — not the Netherlands — ceded Bombay to England. The VOC (Dutch) had no role in the transfer of Bombay.
explanation: Bombay (Mumbai) was ceded by Portugal to England as part of the marriage treaty of Charles II and Catherine of Braganza (1661). The British Crown later handed it to the East India Company in 1668 for an annual rent of £10. The Diwani rights (1765) gave the EIC a vast revenue base in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. The Northern Circars were indeed secured by displacing French influence established by Bussy. Madras was correctly returned at Aix-la-Chapelle (1748).
